entry.narrative_markdown:
## Proof Summary: Parentage of John Richardson, Baptised Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire, 25 September 1832

**Research question:** What does the Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire parish christening register record for John Richardson, baptised 25 September 1833, reveal about his parentage?

**Conclusion (probable):** The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that John Richardson, baptised at St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire, on 25 September 1832, is the son of **Thomas Richardson**, a spinner, and **Mary Richardson, née Mallalieu**, his wife.

---

### Evidence

**Primary source — original baptism register (src_004).** The most direct and weightiest evidence is entry no. 2040 in the original Anglican baptism register of St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne. The entry records:

> No. 2040: September 25 — John [child] — Thomas X Richardson [father], Mary [mother] — Town — Spinner — J. Hardman

The officiating curate, J. Hardman, recorded the entry at the time of the baptism. This source is classified **original** (the register itself, not a copy) with **primary** information (the recording clergyman wrote from contemporaneous knowledge of the event) and constitutes **direct** evidence of both the baptism and parentage: Thomas Richardson and Mary are named as father and mother respectively. Thomas Richardson signed with a mark ("X"), indicating he was present at the baptism. His occupation is given as spinner, consistent with a Lancashire textile-trade household in the 1830s.

Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254–255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674.

**Primary source — original marriage register (src_003).** The original Anglican marriage register of St Leonard, Walton le Dale records at entry no. 684:

> Thos Richardson, Bachelor of this Parish Chapelry and Mary Mallalieu, Spinster of this Parish Chapelry were married in this Chapel by Banns this Twelfth Day of November in the Year One thousand eight hundred and twenty six By me Henry Fielden Sub Curate. Thomas Richardson his mark / Mary Mallalieu her mark. In the Presence of John Quarmen / James Townson.

This source is **original**, **primary**, and **direct** as to the marriage. It identifies Mary's maiden surname as **Mallalieu**, which the baptism register alone does not record. The marriage took place on 12 November 1826, approximately six years before John's 1832 baptism — a plausible interval for a first or early child. Walton le Dale is immediately adjacent to Preston (the birth place recorded in John Richardson's tree entry), which is geographically consistent. Both Thomas and Mary signed with marks, consistent with the baptism register where Thomas also signed with a mark ("X"). This cross-record consistency in literacy level supports the identity correlation.

Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm.

**Derivative sources — FamilySearch indexes (src_001, src_002).** Two FamilySearch index entries corroborate the above. The first, from "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975" (collection 1473014), records John Richardson's christening at Ashton-under-Lyne with father Thomas Richardson and mother Mary.^["England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm.] The second, from "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910" (collection 1465701), records the 1826 marriage of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu at Walton le Dale.^["England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QJDD-R1CZ : 9 March 2024), Entry for Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 Nov 1826; St Leonard, Walton le Dale, Lancashire, England; citing FHL microfilm of original parish register.] Both are **derivative** sources (GSU/FamilySearch indexes derived from FHL microfilms of original registers), providing **secondary** information, and are classified as **direct** evidence of the respective events. They carry less evidentiary weight than the original images already transcribed above but are consistent with those originals in all material particulars.

---

### Source correlation and identity

The four sources above — two original register images and two derivative indexes — agree on all material facts: the child is named John; the father is Thomas Richardson (a spinner who signed by mark); the mother is Mary (maiden name Mallalieu per the marriage register); the baptism took place on 25 September 1832 at Ashton-under-Lyne. The marriage register places the couple in the Preston/Walton le Dale area in 1826, consistent with John's tree-recorded birth place of Preston.

One minor discrepancy exists: the derivative christening index (src_001) and the tree entry both record the baptism year as **1832** (index) or **1833** (tree), respectively, while the original baptism register image (src_004) records the date as 25 September 1832. The day, month, church, and parents are identical across all records. The weight of the original register image (src_004) resolves this discrepancy in favour of 1832: the 1833 tree date is most plausibly a one-year transcription error carried over from an IGI-derived entry. This discrepancy does not affect the parentage conclusion.

---

### Limitations and scope of research

Research was not formally declared exhaustive. The following record types were not searched and could further corroborate the parentage finding: Nonconformist registers for Ashton-under-Lyne and adjacent townships; burial registers; the 1841 and 1851 census returns (which would confirm family co-residence); and records bearing on Thomas Richardson's own origins. These gaps are corroborative in nature — the answer (Thomas Richardson and Mary née Mallalieu are John's parents) is already given directly by two independent original sources. Searching further records would test and strengthen this conclusion but is unlikely to change its substance. The tier is therefore set at **probable** rather than proved, reflecting the absence of a formal exhaustiveness declaration.

---

### Tier declaration

The evidence strongly suggests that John Richardson, baptised at St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne on 25 September 1832, is the son of Thomas Richardson, spinner, and Mary Richardson née Mallalieu. This conclusion rests on two independent original sources — both classified original/primary/direct — that agree on the parentage in every material particular, with corroboration from two derivative indexes and cross-record consistency in literacy markers. The **probable** tier reflects strong preponderance of evidence, with the limitation that research exhaustiveness has not been formally declared and census and other corroborating records remain unsearched.

This source is **original**, **primary**, and **direct** as to the marriage. It identifies Mary's maiden surname as **Mallalieu**, which the baptism register alone does not record. The marriage took place on 12 November 1826, approximately six years before John's 1832 baptism — a plausible interval for a first or early child. Walton le Dale is immediately adjacent to Preston (the birth place recorded in John Richardson's tree entry), which is geographically consistent. Both Thomas and Mary signed with marks, consistent with the baptism register where Thomas also signed with a mark ("X"). This cross-record consistency in literacy level supports the identity correlation.

Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm.

**Derivative sources — FamilySearch indexes (src_001, src_002).** Two FamilySearch index entries corroborate the above. The first, from "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975" (collection 1473014), records John Richardson's christening at Ashton-under-Lyne with father Thomas Richardson and mother Mary.^["England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm.] The second, from "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910" (collection 1465701), records the 1826 marriage of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu at Walton le Dale.^["England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QJDD-R1CZ : 9 March 2024), Entry for Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 Nov 1826; St Leonard, Walton le Dale, Lancashire, England; citing FHL microfilm of original parish register.] Both are **derivative** sources (GSU/FamilySearch indexes derived from FHL microfilms of original registers), providing **secondary** information, and are classified as **direct** evidence of the respective events. They carry less evidentiary weight than the original images already transcribed above but are consistent with those originals in all material particulars.

---

### Source correlation and identity

The four sources above — two original register images and two derivative indexes — agree on all material facts: the child is named John; the father is Thomas Richardson (a spinner who signed by mark); the mother is Mary (maiden name Mallalieu per the marriage register); the baptism took place on 25 September 1832 at Ashton-under-Lyne. The marriage register places the couple in the Preston/Walton le Dale area in 1826, consistent with John's tree-recorded birth place of Preston.

One minor discrepancy exists: the derivative christening index (src_001) and the tree entry both record the baptism year as **1832** (index) or **1833** (tree), respectively, while the original baptism register image (src_004) records the date as 25 September 1832. The day, month, church, and parents are identical across all records. The weight of the original register image (src_004) resolves this discrepancy in favour of 1832: the 1833 tree date is most plausibly a one-year transcription error carried over from an IGI-derived entry. This discrepancy does not affect the parentage conclusion.

---

### Limitations and scope of research

Research was not formally declared exhaustive. The following record types were not searched and could further corroborate the parentage finding: Nonconformist registers for Ashton-under-Lyne and adjacent townships; burial registers; the 1841 and 1851 census returns (which would confirm family co-residence); and records bearing on Thomas Richardson's own origins. These gaps are corroborative in nature — the answer (Thomas Richardson and Mary née Mallalieu are John's parents) is already given directly by two independent original sources. Searching further records would test and strengthen this conclusion but is unlikely to change its substance. The tier is therefore set at **probable** rather than proved, reflecting the absence of a formal exhaustiveness declaration.

---

### Tier declaration

The evidence strongly suggests that John Richardson, baptised at St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne on 25 September 1832, is the son of Thomas Richardson, spinner, and Mary Richardson née Mallalieu. This conclusion rests on two independent original sources — both classified original/primary/direct — that agree on the parentage in every material particular, with corroboration from two derivative indexes and cross-record consistency in literacy markers. The **probable** tier reflects strong preponderance of evidence, with the limitation that research exhaustiveness has not been formally declared and census and other corroborating records remain unsearched.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who Was the Father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?

**Conclusion:** Thomas Flynn is proved to be the father of Patrick Flynn (born approximately 1845 in County Tipperary, Ireland; died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania).

### Evidence

Five independent lines of evidence establish the paternity, including two original sources in which primary informants directly recorded the father-son relationship at or near the time of Patrick's birth.

**1. 1845 Irish Catholic Baptismal Register (strongest evidence)**

The most probative source is the original parish baptismal register of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, County Tipperary, Ireland. The entry, dated 12 March 1845, records the baptism of "Patricius Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan," witnessed by Rev. Michael O'Connor (the officiating priest), with the parents and godparents present at the ceremony. This is an original record (an actual parish register page, not a derivative) providing primary information — the parents named themselves to the priest, who recorded the entry in his official capacity with no incentive to misrecord. The informant proximity is "witness": the priest observed the parents directly.

*Citation:* St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church (County Tipperary, Ireland), baptismal register, entry for Patricius Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan, baptized 12 March 1845; National Library of Ireland Catholic Parish Registers, microfilm 04173/04, image 287; digital image, NationalLibrary.ie, accessed 4 May 2026. [a_014]

**2. Flynn Family Bible Birth Entry (second independent primary-information source)**

The Flynn family Bible (Holy Bible, Dublin imprint 1840) contains a birth-record page recording Patrick Flynn, born 1845, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan. The entries are in a single consistent contemporaneous hand, and the 1840 Bible imprint predates all entries, which together support that births were recorded as they occurred rather than transcribed later. The recorder was Thomas Flynn himself, the father, who had firsthand knowledge of his children's births. This source is original (the physical Bible), provides primary information (the father recording his own son's birth), and is fully independent of the baptismal register — different recorder, different record type, different institution. The father had no incentive to misrecord his own child's parentage.

*Citation:* Flynn family Bible (Holy Bible, Dublin imprint 1840), birth and family record pages, entry for Patrick Flynn, b. 1845, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan; original privately held by a Flynn descendant; digital images examined 4 May 2026. [a_015]

**3. 1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate (direct evidence, secondary informant)**

Patrick Flynn's death certificate, no. 4521, dated 1908, lists "Thomas Flynn" as Patrick's father. The informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law — a family member not present at Patrick's birth and reporting parentage information secondhand, decades after the event. This is direct evidence of the relationship (it names the father explicitly) but secondary information (the informant did not witness Patrick's birth). As a secondary informant, James Brown's account carries less weight than the two primary sources above, but it corroborates the same conclusion independently. The same death certificate erroneously records Patrick's birthplace as Pennsylvania rather than Ireland — attributable to the son-in-law's likely unfamiliarity with the circumstances of Patrick's birth abroad — but this discrepancy, addressed under the birthplace conflict (now resolved), does not affect the paternity conclusion.

*Citation:* Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. [a_013]

**4. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (indirect corroboration)**

The 1850 federal census enumerates Patrick Flynn (age 5, born Ireland) in the household of Thomas Flynn (head, age ~32) in Schuylkill County, dwelling 84, family 91. The 1850 census does not record explicit relationships — the father-son relationship is inferred from Patrick's age (consistent with a birth of ~1845), shared surname, and position in the household. ## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

However, the census informants are likely the same household member (Thomas Flynn or wife), so the two census assertions may share a single informant — potentially not fully independent for this fact.
items.weighing_analysis: The census records are contemporary recordings made near the time of Patrick's birth, while the death certificate was created 63 years later. The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.
items.resolution_rationale: Ireland is accepted as the birthplace. The 1908 death certificate birthplace of 'Pennsylvania' is rejected as a likely error by the son-in-law informant, who may have confused Patrick's place of residence with his place of birth, or may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland before immigrating as a young child.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Proof Summary: Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)

### Research Question

Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born approximately 1845 in Ireland (per census records), who died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

### Conclusion

The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that **Thomas Flynn** was the father of Patrick Flynn. No evidence currently identifies Patrick Flynn's mother. Accordingly, paternity is concluded at the **probable** tier; maternity is **not proved**.

### Evidence — Paternity

**1850 U.S. Federal Census (indirect, indeterminate information quality).**
The 1850 federal census for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 84, family 91, lists Thomas Flynn as head of household, with a child named Patrick Flynn, age 5, born in Ireland.[^1] The 1850 census does not record family relationships — enumeration of Patrick in the Thomas Flynn household is indirect evidence inferred from shared surname and household position, not a stated relationship. The informant is unknown; for names, ages, and birthplaces, a household member (most likely Thomas Flynn himself) presumably provided the information, but the census does not identify the informant. This evidence is classified as: *original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence.*

**1860 U.S. Federal Census (indirect, indeterminate information quality).**
The 1860 federal census for Schuylkill County, dwelling 112, family 119, lists Thomas Flynn as head of household, with Patrick Flynn, age 15, born in Ireland.[^2] As with the 1850 census, no relationship column existed in 1860; the father-son connection is inferred from Patrick's age (consistent with the 1850 enumeration), shared surname, and continued enumeration in the same household. The informant is unknown. This evidence is classified as: *original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence.*

Taken together, the two census co-enumerations establish a consistent pattern across a decade: Patrick Flynn, whose age progression is mutually corroborating (~1845 birth in Ireland → age 5 in 1850 → age 15 in 1860), resided continuously in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The shared surname, consistent birthplace (Ireland), and geographic stability strengthen the inference that Thomas was Patrick's father, rather than a boarder, employer, or other non-familial head.

**1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate (direct, secondary information quality).**
Pennsylvania death certificate no. 4521, issued 14 March 1908 for Patrick Flynn of Schuylkill County, states the father's name as Thomas Flynn.[^3] The informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law, Brown had no direct knowledge of Patrick's parentage (he was not present at Patrick's birth and learned this information secondhand); his information is accordingly classified as secondary. The death certificate is classified as: *original source; secondary information (for parentage facts); direct evidence.* The secondary nature of the informant reduces the weight of this record for the paternity question, but it corroborates the census-based inference and names Thomas Flynn explicitly.

### Correlation of Paternity Evidence

The three sources are independent — two federal censuses and a state vital record — and all are consistent in identifying Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County as the head of the household in which Patrick Flynn lived as a child, and as Patrick's named father at death. No source contradicts this identification. The convergence of two independent census enumerations (indirect) and an explicit death certificate statement (direct but secondary) constitutes a strong preponderance of evidence supporting Thomas Flynn's paternity.

The probable tier (rather than proved) is selected because: (1) research was not declared exhaustive — the 1870 and 1880 censuses, probate records, and a marriage record for Patrick were not searched; (2) the 1880 census, which explicitly records relationships, could provide direct-primary evidence and was not consulted; (3) all parentage evidence is either indirect or direct-but-secondary; and (4) the death certificate informant was not present at Patrick's birth and reported secondhand knowledge.

### Evidence — Maternity

No assertion in the current record set names Patrick Flynn's mother. No woman is linked by person_evidence to Patrick as mother. The 1850 and 1860 censuses may have listed a woman in the Thomas Flynn household, but no such assertions were extracted for question q_001, and no death certificate entry names a mother. Maternity is accordingly **not proved**. Records that could establish the mother's identity include: the 1850 and 1860 census enumerations in the Thomas Flynn household (a woman of appropriate age sharing the household would be a candidate); Schuylkill County church records (Catholic parishes serving the Irish immigrant community); Patrick Flynn's marriage record (which may name his parents); and Schuylkill County probate records for Thomas Flynn.

### Limitations and Next Steps

The research gaps are significant. The 1880 U.S. census — the first to record relationships explicitly — was not searched for Patrick or Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County and could independently confirm the father-son relationship. The 1870 and 1900 censuses were similarly not searched. No marriage record for Patrick Flynn was located, which may name his parents. Probate records for Thomas Flynn were not searched. Until these sources are consulted, the parentage conclusion rests on corroborating but indirect and secondary evidence.

Notwithstanding these gaps, the convergence of three independent sources over two decades, all consistently pointing to Thomas Flynn, supports a probable conclusion for paternity at this stage of research.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Proof Summary: Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, Ireland, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, PA)

### Research Question

Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born approximately 1845 in Ireland (per census records), who died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

### Conclusion

The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that **Thomas Flynn** was the father of Patrick Flynn. No evidence currently identifies Patrick Flynn's mother. Paternity is concluded at the **probable** tier; maternity is **not proved** on the present evidence.

---

### Evidence — Paternity

**1850 U.S. Federal Census (indirect evidence; indeterminate information quality).**
The 1850 federal census for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 84, family 91, lists Thomas Flynn as head of household, with Patrick Flynn, age 5, born in Ireland, enumerated in that household.[^1] The 1850 census does not record family relationships — Patrick's enumeration in Thomas Flynn's household is indirect evidence, inferred from shared surname and household position rather than from a stated relationship. The informant for ages and birthplaces is unknown; as head of household, Thomas Flynn presumably provided most details, but the census does not name the informant. This evidence is classified as: *original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence.*

**1860 U.S. Federal Census (indirect evidence; indeterminate information quality).**
The 1860 federal census for Schuylkill County, dwelling 112, family 119, again lists Thomas Flynn as head of household, with Patrick Flynn, age 15, born in Ireland.[^2] No relationship column existed in the 1860 census (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880); the father-son inference rests on the same basis as in 1850 — shared surname, consistent age progression (~1845 birth; age 5 in 1850; age 15 in 1860), and continued enumeration in the same household in the same county. The informant is unknown. This evidence is classified as: *original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence.*

Taken together, the two census enumerations establish a consistent pattern over a decade: Patrick Flynn (age progression corroborated across both enumerations) resided continuously in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. The shared surname, consistent Ireland birthplace, geographic stability, and age corroboration strengthen the inference that Thomas was Patrick's father rather than a boarder, employer, or other non-familial household head.

**1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate (direct evidence; secondary information quality).**
Pennsylvania death certificate no. 4521, issued 14 March 1908 for Patrick Flynn of Schuylkill County, explicitly names Thomas Flynn as the father.[^3] The informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law, Brown had no direct knowledge of Patrick's parentage — he was not present at Patrick's birth and learned this information secondhand. His testimony on parentage is accordingly classified as secondary. The certificate is classified as: *original source; secondary information (for parentage and birth facts); direct evidence.* The secondary nature of the informant reduces the evidentiary weight of this record for the paternity question, but it corroborates the census-based inference and names Thomas Flynn explicitly in a legal instrument.

### Correlation

The three sources are independent — two federal censuses and a Pennsylvania vital record — and all consistently identify Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County as the household head in which Patrick Flynn was enumerated as a child, and as Patrick's named father at death. No source contradicts this identification. The convergence of two independent census enumerations (indirect) with an explicit death certificate statement (direct, secondary informant) constitutes a strong preponderance of evidence supporting Thomas Flynn's paternity.

### Tier Rationale

Paternity is concluded at **probable** (not proved) for the following reasons:

1. Research was not declared exhaustive. The 1870 and 1880 federal censuses, Patrick Flynn's marriage record, Schuylkill County probate records for Thomas Flynn, and Irish parish or civil registers were not searched.
2. The 1880 census — the first to record stated relationships — was not consulted and could provide direct-primary evidence of the father-son relationship, or evidence narrowing the conclusion.
3. All parentage evidence is either indirect (census co-enumerations) or direct-but-secondary (death certificate via son-in-law informant). No direct-primary evidence of parentage (e.g., a baptism record or a 1880 census entry stating "son") has been located.

Notwithstanding these gaps, the corroboration across three independent sources over nearly sixty years supports a probable conclusion for paternity at this stage of research.

### Evidence — Maternity

No assertion in the current record set names Patrick Flynn's mother. No source consulted in this research effort names a woman in the role of Patrick's mother. Maternity is accordingly **not proved**. Records that could establish the mother's identity include: the full enumeration of the Thomas Flynn household in the 1850 and 1860 censuses (a woman of appropriate age sharing the household would be a candidate); Schuylkill County or Irish Catholic parish baptism registers; Patrick Flynn's marriage record (which may name his parents); and Schuylkill County probate records for Thomas Flynn.

### Limitations and Next Steps

The 1880 U.S. census — which explicitly records relationships and was not searched — is the single highest-priority record for advancing this conclusion. A search for Patrick Flynn (and for Thomas Flynn, if then living) in Schuylkill County in 1880 could independently confirm the father-son relationship with primary-direct evidence, or surface a contradiction. The 1870 and 1900 censuses and Patrick Flynn's marriage record are also important unsearched sources. Until these are consulted, the conclusion rests on corroborating but indirect and secondary evidence.

---

[^2]: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

[^3]: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Proof Argument: Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)

### Research Question

Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born approximately 1845 (census evidence indicates Ireland as the birth country, contradicting the 1908 death certificate's notation of Pennsylvania), who died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

### Summary of Conclusion

The evidence strongly suggests that **Thomas Flynn** (I2) was Patrick Flynn's father — a finding this argument places at **probable**. The identity of Patrick's mother remains unresolved at **possible**: a Bridget Flynn, enumerated as a widow in Schuylkill County in 1870, is the only maternal candidate located, but no record directly connects her to Thomas Flynn or to Patrick Flynn. The two claims are assessed independently below.

---

### Source Analysis

**Source 1 — 1850 U.S. Census, Thomas Flynn household (src_001)**
"1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026."

This is an **original** source (the census enumeration itself). The information bearing on Patrick's parentage is **indeterminate** as to quality: the 1850 census lists no relationship column — household position and shared surname yield an *inferred* parent-child relationship, not a stated one. The evidence for parentage is therefore **indirect**. The informant is unknown; Thomas Flynn likely provided his own name as head, but no informant is identified for other household members. A child named Patrick Flynn, age 5, appears at a position consistent with being Thomas's son.

**Source 2 — 1860 U.S. Census, Thomas Flynn household (src_003)**
"1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026."

Also an **original** source. As in 1850, the 1860 census states no relationships — the relationship column was not introduced until the 1880 census. The information is **indeterminate** in quality; the evidence for parentage is **indirect**. A Patrick Flynn, age 15 (birth year ~1845), appears in the same household as Thomas Flynn (I2) in the same county ten years after the 1850 enumeration. The age is exactly consistent with the 1850 entry.

**Source 3 — 1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate, Patrick Flynn (src_004)**
"Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026."

An **original** source (a government-created vital record). The informant is **James Brown, son-in-law** — a family member not present at Patrick's birth; the parentage information is therefore **secondary** in quality. The certificate names "Thomas Flynn" as Patrick's father. The evidence for this fact is **direct**: the certificate explicitly states the father's name. Note that the death certificate gives Pennsylvania as Patrick's birthplace, while both censuses record Ireland — a discrepancy consistent with a son-in-law who may not have had accurate knowledge of his father-in-law's origins. This discrepancy does not affect the paternity finding but underscores the limits of the informant's knowledge.

**Source 4 — 1870 U.S. Census, Bridget Flynn household (src_005)**
"1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026."

An **original** source. The information is **indeterminate** in quality. A woman named Bridget Flynn, age 52 (born ~1818), is enumerated as a widow and head of household in Schuylkill County in 1870. No children are enumerated in her household (consistent with Patrick, then approximately 25, having already established his own household). The record identifies neither her late husband by name nor any of her children. The evidence bearing on maternity is **indirect**: the connection to Thomas Flynn and to Patrick is inferred from the shared surname and the timing of her widowhood, not from any stated relationship.

---

### Paternity: Thomas Flynn (Probable)

Three independent pieces of evidence converge on Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father.

First, the 1850 census (src_001, a_004, a_005) places a Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — a position consistent with a father-son relationship, though not explicitly stated by the record.

Second, the 1860 census (src_003, a_008, a_010) places a Patrick Flynn, age 15, in the same Thomas Flynn household in the same county. The ages across the two censuses are exactly consistent (age 5 in 1850, age 15 in 1860, birth year ~1845 in both). The fact that the same Patrick Flynn appears in the same Thomas Flynn household a full decade later is significant corroborating evidence that this is not a coincidental same-name enumeration.

Third, and most directly, Patrick Flynn's 1908 death certificate (src_004, a_013) explicitly names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant, James Brown (son-in-law), is secondary — he was not present at Patrick's birth and reports parentage as told to him. The direct statement, however, is consistent with and supported by the two decades of census co-residence.

Taken together, two independent original census records provide indirect corroborating evidence of a parent-child household relationship, and a death certificate provides a direct (if secondary-informant) naming. No evidence contradicts this paternity. The 1860 census, as a second independent original source, independently corroborates the 1850 evidence and reduces the probability of coincidental co-enumeration. The paternity conclusion is assessed at **probable**: the preponderance of evidence points strongly to Thomas Flynn as father, but research has not been declared exhaustive — probate records for Thomas Flynn and church baptism registers remain unsearched and could further confirm (or in an unlikely scenario, refute) this link.

---

### Maternity: Bridget Flynn (Possible Only)

The maternal claim rests entirely on two assertions from the 1870 Schuylkill County census (src_005): that a woman named Bridget Flynn (a_014) is enumerated as a widow (a_015) in the same county where Thomas Flynn's family resided. The person_evidence link for Bridget Flynn (I3) is rated *speculative* with a match score of 0.0002.

The hypothesis that this Bridget is Patrick's mother (h_002) requires the following chain of inference: (1) Bridget Flynn was married to Thomas Flynn (I2); (2) Thomas Flynn died between 1860 (when he appeared in the census) and 1870 (when Bridget appears as a widow); (3) this particular Bridget Flynn, among all women of that name in Schuylkill County, is the specific widow of Thomas Flynn.

None of these steps is established by any record in hand. "Flynn" is a common Irish surname throughout Schuylkill County's coal-region communities. No marriage record for Thomas Flynn and any Bridget has been located. No death record for Thomas Flynn has been located. No record names Bridget Flynn as Patrick's mother or as Thomas Flynn's wife. The 1870 census entry for Bridget names no late husband and enumerates no children.

The 1860 census (src_003) is particularly notable in this respect: if Thomas Flynn had a wife named Bridget, she would be expected to appear in his 1860 household. The 1860 census entry for Thomas Flynn's household has not been described as including a wife — this is a significant gap in the maternal hypothesis.

The maternity claim is therefore assessed at **possible**: a credible hypothesis that cannot be ruled out, but for which no record provides positive identification. Recording it at a higher tier would rest on a same-surname coincidence alone — precisely the weak-identity pattern the person_evidence assessment warns against.

Records that could resolve the maternity question include: a marriage record for Thomas and Bridget Flynn in Schuylkill County or Ireland; Thomas Flynn's death record (naming a survivor or family); church baptism records for Patrick Flynn naming both parents; the 1860 census enumeration of Thomas Flynn's wife; or probate records for Thomas Flynn naming his widow.

---

### Research Scope and Exhaustiveness

The exhaustive declaration has not been formally made for this question. Records searched include: the 1850 U.S. Federal Census (FamilySearch, NARA M432), the 1860 U.S. Federal Census (FamilySearch, NARA M653), the 1870 U.S. Federal Census (FamilySearch, NARA M593), and the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate for Patrick Flynn (Pennsylvania State Archives via FamilySearch). An Ancestry.com derivative index of the 1850 census was also consulted and found consistent with the FamilySearch image.

Records not yet searched include probate records for Thomas Flynn (Schuylkill County Orphans' Court), Catholic and other church baptism and marriage registers in Schuylkill County (most likely St. Clair or Minersville parishes), the 1880 and 1900 U.S. censuses for Patrick Flynn's own household (which might name a mother still living), and Pennsylvania naturalization records. A marriage record for Thomas Flynn and Bridget — if found — would transform the maternal claim from possible to probable or proved. Until these sources are searched, the research cannot be declared exhaustive, and both conclusions are held below the Proved threshold.

---

### Conclusion

The evidence **strongly suggests** that Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) was the son of **Thomas Flynn** of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. This paternal conclusion is assessed at **probable**: two independent original census records corroborate a decade-long co-residence, and a death certificate directly names Thomas as father. The identity of Patrick's mother is assessed at **possible**: Bridget Flynn, enumerated as a widow in Schuylkill County in 1870, is the only maternal candidate identified, but no record connects her to Thomas Flynn or to Patrick. The paternal conclusion is suitable for encoding in the research tree as a sourced ParentChild relationship at probable confidence; the maternal link is not yet appropriate for encoding at that tier.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who Were the Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?

### Research Question

This proof summary addresses the question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born approximately 1845, believed to be in Pennsylvania, and died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

### Conclusion

The preponderance of available evidence strongly suggests that **Thomas Flynn** was the father of Patrick Flynn. No mother has been identified in the records searched to date. This conclusion is assessed at the **probable** tier: multiple independent sources are consistent and corroborating, but research has not been declared exhaustive and the direct parentage evidence comes from a secondary informant. No alternative candidate father was identified in any record examined.

### Sources and Evidence

**1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania** (original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence of relationship)

The 1850 federal census for Schuylkill County enumerates a household headed by Thomas Flynn, age approximately 32, born Ireland. A child named Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the same dwelling (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census did not record relationships between household members — the relationship between Patrick and Thomas is therefore inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly stated.^1 This is indirect evidence: a researcher-constructed inference from household structure, not information provided by an identifiable informant.

**1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania** (original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence of relationship)

Ten years later, the 1860 federal census for the same county enumerates Thomas Flynn's household again (dwelling 112, family 119), now including a Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland.^2 The age and birthplace of this Patrick are consistent with the child enumerated in 1850 (age 5, born Ireland), and his continued co-enumeration in Thomas Flynn's household across two census years strengthens the inference of a parent-child relationship. Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census did not record household relationships; the conclusion again rests on position, shared surname, and age consistency.

**Pennsylvania Death Certificate No. 4521 (1908)** (original source; secondary information; direct evidence of relationship)

The death certificate of Patrick Flynn, dated 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, was completed by informant James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law.^3 Brown named Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father. This is the only record in the searched set that directly states the father-son relationship. Because James Brown was not present at Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told or knew about his father-in-law's parentage, this information is classified as **secondary**: reliable for what a family member knew, but not original knowledge. Brown also reported Patrick's birthplace as Pennsylvania, which conflicts with both the 1850 and 1860 census entries naming Ireland as the birthplace. This discrepancy does not bear on the paternity conclusion — it reflects the limits of the son-in-law's knowledge of his father-in-law's early life — but it is noted as an indicator that Brown's secondary information should be weighed carefully.

### Correlation and Weight of Evidence

All three records are mutually consistent on the core question of paternity. The 1850 and 1860 census enumerations place a child named Patrick Flynn, of consistent age and Irish birth, in the same Thomas Flynn household in Schuylkill County across two independent enumerations a decade apart. The death certificate's naming of Thomas Flynn as father is the only direct statement of the relationship, and it accords with the household evidence. No record examined names any other person as Patrick's father, and no competing candidate was identified.

The weakness of the evidence is threefold. First, both census entries provide only indirect evidence of the relationship — household co-enumeration without an explicit relationship column. Second, the sole direct statement of paternity comes from a secondary informant (son-in-law James Brown), whose reliability on facts about his father-in-law's birth and parentage is reduced by generational distance. Third, several record types that could independently confirm or further establish the relationship — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses for Patrick, Schuylkill County church registers, probate records, and naturalization papers — were not searched in this phase.

### Mother Not Identified

No record in the set searched names Patrick Flynn's mother. The 1850 and 1860 census households undoubtedly included a woman who may have been Patrick's mother, but her name and relationship to Patrick are not captured in the parentage assertion. The death certificate lists only the father. Research into Patrick's mother's identity remains open.

### Exhaustiveness

Research has **not** been declared exhaustive. The 1870, 1880, and 1900 U.S. federal censuses for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County were not searched. Schuylkill County probate records, church baptismal registers, and naturalization records — all of which might name parents directly or confirm family relationships — were not consulted in this research phase. The unsearched records are expected primarily to corroborate the paternity conclusion already supported by three consistent sources, rather than to introduce a competing candidate. This expectation, however, does not substitute for the searches themselves.

### Tier Declaration

This conclusion is assessed at the **probable** tier. The evidence strongly suggests Thomas Flynn was Patrick Flynn's father: three independent records from two distinct record types are consistent, no alternative candidate appears in any record examined, and the direct naming of Thomas Flynn on the death certificate corroborates the household co-enumeration evidence. The tier falls short of proved because GPS Component 1 (reasonably exhaustive research) is not fully met, and the only direct relationship evidence comes from a secondary informant. The conclusion should be revisited when the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses and Schuylkill County probate and church records have been searched.

---

^1 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.

^2 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

^3 Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly encoded the probable-tier conclusion on the tree. The ParentChild relationship (R1) was added via tree_edit with Thomas Flynn (I2) as parent and Patrick Flynn (I1) as child. The relationship carries three source references: S3 (death certificate, quality 2—secondary informant), S1 (1850 census, quality 1—indirect), and S2 (1860 census, quality 1—indirect). The relationship is sourced (non-null refs), and the quality ratings appropriately reflect the evidence type (secondary for direct statement, indirect for census co-residence). The concluded relationship now appears on the tree, not merely in the narrative. The encoding follows the spec for a case where the edge did not previously exist.
